questions.question: Picture a coordinate grid: both the x-axis and the y-axis are numbered from −6 to 6, one square is 1 unit, and the two axes cross at the origin (0, 0). Point P sits 3 units to the right of the origin and 5 units up. What ordered pair names point P?
questions.explain: In Cartesian coordinates the first number is always the x-move (right/left) and the second is the y-move (up/down), so 3 right and 5 up is (3, 5). The usual trap is writing the pair backwards as (5, 3), which lands you 5 right and 3 up instead.

questions.question: On that same grid (x-axis and y-axis numbered from −6 to 6, one square = 1 unit, axes crossing at the origin), point Q sits 4 units to the left of the origin and 2 units up. Which quadrant is Q in?
options: Quadrant IV
Quadrant II
Quadrant III
Quadrant I
questions.explain: Left of the origin means x is negative and up means y is positive, and the quadrant with a negative x and a positive y is Quadrant II (the top-left one). Watch out: reading the pair backwards as 4 up and 2 right would wrongly send you to Quadrant I or IV.

questions.question: On the same coordinate grid (both axes numbered from −6 to 6, one square = 1 unit, origin where the axes cross), point R sits 0 units to the right or left of the origin and 4 units up. Which statement about R is correct?
options: R is (4, 0) and sits on the x-axis
R is (0, 4) and sits inside Quadrant I
R is (0, 4), sits on the y-axis, and is in no quadrant
R is (0, −4) and sits on the y-axis
questions.explain: No sideways move means x = 0, and 4 up means y = 4, so R is (0, 4); a point sitting on an axis is on the border and belongs to no quadrant. The common trap is calling any point that is up and not-left 'Quadrant I' — quadrants are the four open regions between the axes.

questions.question: On the same coordinate grid (axes numbered from −6 to 6, one square = 1 unit, origin at the crossing point), point S sits 5 units to the left of the origin and 3 units down. Which pair and quadrant are both correct for S?
options: (−5, 3), Quadrant II
(−3, −5), Quadrant III
(5, −3), Quadrant IV
(−5, −3), Quadrant III
questions.explain: Left makes the x-value −5 and down makes the y-value −3, giving (−5, −3), and two negatives put a point in Quadrant III (bottom-left). The trap is swapping the numbers to (−3, −5); that pair also looks like Quadrant III but it marks a different spot on the grid.

questions.question: Which of these points lies in Quadrant IV?
questions.explain: Quadrant IV is the bottom-right region, so its points have a positive x and a negative y, which matches (8, −3). A frequent slip is grabbing (−8, 3) because it has a negative sign somewhere — the position of the negative sign is what decides the quadrant.

questions.question: On a map of Priya's neighbourhood in Kelowna, the origin (0, 0) is her school. One unit east is +1 on the x-axis and one unit north is +1 on the y-axis; each unit is 1 block. Priya's home is 6 blocks east and 4 blocks south of the school. Which ordered pair gives her home?
questions.explain: East is the x-direction, so 6 blocks east gives x = 6, and south is the opposite of north, so 4 blocks south gives y = −4, making (6, −4). The two usual traps are writing the north–south number first and forgetting that south flips the sign of y.

questions.question: Four points are marked on a grid: (−4, −7), (−9, −2), (−1, −6), and (−3, 6). Which one is NOT in the same quadrant as the other three?
questions.explain: Check the sign pair of each point: negative x with negative y is Quadrant III, so the three bottom-left points match and (−3, 6) is the odd one out in Quadrant II. Do not sort by size of the numbers — only the signs tell you the quadrant.

questions.question: Jaya plots the two points (0, −6) and (−6, 0) on a coordinate grid. Which statement about them is true?
options: Both points are in Quadrant III, because both use a 6 and a 0.
(0, −6) is in Quadrant IV and (−6, 0) is in Quadrant II.
(0, −6) is on the x-axis and (−6, 0) is on the y-axis.
(0, −6) is on the y-axis and (−6, 0) is on the x-axis, so neither point is in a quadrant.
questions.explain: A zero x-value means no sideways move, so the point stays on the vertical y-axis, and a zero y-value keeps the point on the horizontal x-axis; axis points are in no quadrant. The trap is mixing up which zero pins you to which axis — the first number controls left/right.

questions.question: At a skate park in Burnaby, the map has the origin at the water fountain, with +x metres east and +y metres north. A bench is recorded at (−8, 5). Owen says the bench must be in Quadrant IV. Which statement correctly fixes his thinking?
options: The bench is in Quadrant II: −8 means 8 m west of the fountain and 5 means 5 m north, so it is left of the y-axis and above the x-axis.
The bench is in Quadrant IV: a negative first number always drops a point below the x-axis.
The bench is in Quadrant I: the negative sign only tells you the distance, not the direction.
The bench is in Quadrant III: the pair should be read as 8 down and 5 left.
questions.explain: Take the numbers one at a time — the first number moves you east or west and the second moves you north or south, so (−8, 5) is west and north, which is the top-left region, Quadrant II. The classic error is letting one negative sign push the whole point downward; only the y-value controls up and down.

questions.question: For a treasure-hunt game in class, Sam should mark the treasure at (−3, 7), but he writes the marker at (7, −3) instead. Which statement best describes what his mistake did?
options: Both points are in Quadrant II, because they use the same two numbers.
(−3, 7) is in Quadrant II but (7, −3) is in Quadrant IV, so swapping the numbers moved the marker into a different quadrant.
Both points are in Quadrant IV, because each pair has one negative number.
(−3, 7) is in Quadrant IV and (7, −3) is in Quadrant II.
questions.explain: Read each pair as x first then y: negative x with positive y is the top-left region (Quadrant II), while positive x with negative y is the bottom-right region (Quadrant IV). Using the same two numbers does not mean the same point — order changes both the position and the quadrant.

questions.question: A drone starts at the origin of a grid over a field in Abbotsford, where +x is east and +y is north and one unit is 1 metre. It flies 6 m east, then 9 m north, then 10 m west, and stops. What are the drone's coordinates and which quadrant is it in?
options: (9, −4), Quadrant IV
(−4, 9), Quadrant III
(−4, 9), Quadrant II
(4, 9), Quadrant I
questions.explain: Track the two directions separately: east–west gives 6 − 10 = −4 for x, and north–south gives 9 for y, so the drone is at (−4, 9), which is left of the y-axis and above the x-axis — Quadrant II. The trap is reporting the north number first or dropping the negative sign on x after flying back past the start.

questions.question: On a harbour grid in Victoria the origin is the tide gauge, +x is east and +y is north. A buoy is logged at (7, −5). Ana says: since 7 is bigger than 5, the buoy must be in Quadrant I. Which statement corrects her?
options: Quadrant I is right, because the larger number in the pair decides the quadrant.
Quadrant II, because the pair means 7 units up and 5 units left of the gauge.
Quadrant III, because any ordered pair containing a negative number is in Quadrant III.
Quadrant IV, because the 7 moves the buoy right of the y-axis and the −5 moves it below the x-axis.
questions.explain: Quadrants are decided by the signs of the two coordinates, never by which number is larger: positive x with negative y is the bottom-right region, Quadrant IV. Also keep the order straight — the first number is the east–west move, so (7, −5) is not the same as 7 up and 5 left.
